filename: Unexpected decline in the ocean carbon sink under record-high sea surface temperatures in 2023.pdf
title: Unexpected decline in the ocean carbon sink under record-high sea surface temperatures in 2023
processes: marine heatwaves and sea surface temperature extremes
code_availability: All code required to perform the analysis and prepare the figures presented in this study is available via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15607822 (ref. 51).
testbed_rationale: The study conducts retrospective and diagnostic carbon flux attribution using existing observation-based statistical/ML products and coarse GOBM simulations rather than producing a reusable training dataset or testbed for physical parameterization development.
pain_points: Severe data sparsity in high-latitude biomes (Southern Ocean and Arctic) results in large ensemble spread and high uncertainty across observation-based products.
Latency of in situ observational data availability requires evaluating out-of-sample near-real-time (NRT) extrapolations beyond training years.
Global ocean biogeochemical models (GOBMs) underestimate non-thermal fCO2 compensating mechanisms in seasonally stratified biomes (such as NA-SPSS) relative to observation-based products.
extraction_notes: Author Galen A. McKinley acknowledges support from the NSF LEAP STC (AGS2019625). The study focuses on using existing ML-mapped observational products to diagnose the 2023 air-sea CO2 flux anomaly rather than developing novel ML parameterization schemes.
